questions.title: Why ACL Evaluation Is AND, Not OR, Across Applicable Rules
questions.prompt: Explain precisely why, when more than one ACL applies to the same read/write/create/delete attempt in ServiceNow, access is denied unless every applicable ACL passes. Why does this surprise new admins, and what real consequence does it have when a narrower ACL is added later to tighten security on a table that already has broader ACLs on it?
questions.modelAnswer: Every ACL record lives on sys_security_acl, and when a user attempts an operation, the platform gathers every ACL whose table, field, and operation match that attempt, then requires all of them to pass — an AND relationship, never an OR. New admins instinctively expect 'if any ACL grants access, they're in,' because that's how permission systems in many other tools work, but ServiceNow's model is the opposite: one failing applicable ACL is enough to deny the whole operation regardless of how many others would have allowed it. The real consequence is that adding a new, narrower ACL never weakens existing access — it can only add a new condition to the AND chain. If that new ACL's role requirement, condition, or script doesn't match a user who previously had access through a broader rule, that user's access breaks, even though nothing about the broader ACL changed and the new rule was never intended to touch their case.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with the AND framing directly: ServiceNow doesn't look for one ACL that says yes, it checks every ACL that applies and all of them have to say yes. That trips people up because most access systems feel additive — more rules usually mean more ways in. Here it's the reverse: more applicable rules mean more hurdles. So when someone bolts on a tight ACL to lock down one field, they're not just adding a new restriction for the people they're targeting — they're adding a new condition that absolutely everyone accessing that table or field now has to clear, including users who were never the intended audience for the new rule.
commonMistakes: Assuming access is granted if any single applicable ACL passes
Not realizing a brand-new ACL can silently break access that previously worked, with no change to the original ACL
Treating 'no ACL exists for this' and 'an ACL exists and fails' as the same outcome
Forgetting that table-level and field-level ACLs both apply and both must pass
keyPoints: All applicable ACLs are evaluated with AND, never OR
A single failing ACL denies the whole operation
Adding a new ACL can never weaken existing access, only add a new condition to clear
This is why 'access broke for an unrelated reason' often traces to a newly added, narrowly-scoped ACL

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the AND relationship across applicable ACLs
Explains why this differs from new admins' intuition
Correctly identifies the consequence of adding a new, narrower ACL
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: How Role, Condition, and Script Combine on a Single ACL
questions.prompt: An ACL lists the itil role in "Requires role" and also has a script that sets answer = false for a specific record. A user holds the itil role. Explain exactly whether this user passes the ACL, and generalize the rule for how role, condition, and script combine within one ACL record versus how multiple ACL records combine with each other.
questions.modelAnswer: The user does not pass this ACL. Holding a listed role only satisfies the role requirement; when an ACL also has a condition or a script, both the role check and the condition/script check must pass — it is an AND within the single ACL record, not an either/or. Since the script explicitly sets answer = false for this record, that half of the check fails, and the user is denied regardless of holding itil. Generalizing: at the record level, role + condition/script combine with AND on one ACL, and that same AND logic also governs how multiple separate ACL records combine with each other when more than one applies to the same operation. It's AND all the way down — within one ACL's ingredients, and across every applicable ACL.
questions.professionalAnswer: Holding the role isn't enough by itself once a script is also present — both pieces have to clear. The role requirement and the script are two separate gates on the same ACL, and this one's script explicitly says no for this record, so the user is denied even with the right role. I'd point out that this is the same AND pattern that governs how separate ACLs stack on top of each other — ServiceNow is consistent about this at every layer: nothing short-circuits to a pass, everything that applies has to agree.
commonMistakes: Assuming holding the required role is sufficient even when a script or condition is also present
Treating role and script as alternative paths to passing rather than both being required
Not recognizing that this AND logic is the same pattern governing multi-ACL evaluation
keyPoints: Role, condition, and script on one ACL combine with AND, not OR
A user can hold every required role and still fail the ACL if the script sets answer = false
This mirrors the AND relationship across separate applicable ACLs
A script must explicitly set answer; there is no implicit pass

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly concludes the user is denied and explains why
Correctly generalizes the role+condition/script AND rule
Connects this to the multi-ACL AND rule
Clear, precise explanation

questions.title: Why CSDM Is a Reference Framework, Not a Feature Flag
questions.prompt: A junior admin describes CSDM as "a setting you turn on in CMDB Properties." Correct this misconception precisely: what kind of thing is CSDM actually, what specific, expensive problem did it exist to solve across ITSM, ITOM, and Service Portfolio Management, and what concretely changes about how an implementer models data once CSDM is adopted?
questions.modelAnswer: CSDM is a published, vendor-maintained reference framework — documentation and a recommended structure for how CIs, applications, and services relate — not a module or checkbox. Before it existed, every module (ITSM, ITOM, Service Portfolio Management) and every implementation team built its own ad hoc idea of what a 'service' or 'application' record should look like, which caused two expensive, real problems: inside one instance, data shaped for one module's expectations often didn't match what another module needed, so dashboards and reports silently misread or missed records; and across customers, every implementation partner re-derived its own structure from scratch, so lessons learned never transferred between engagements or jobs. Adopting CSDM means an implementer stops inventing their own shapes for services, applications, and infrastructure, and instead models data against CSDM's documented domains and vocabulary, so every module and every future implementer can read and write against the same shared contract.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd correct that directly — there's no toggle. CSDM is a documented, standard way of structuring CMDB, application, and service data that ServiceNow publishes and every implementation is supposed to follow, precisely because the alternative — every team inventing its own model — was genuinely expensive. Reports built for one module couldn't reliably read data shaped for another, and knowledge never transferred between engagements because everyone's model was bespoke. Adopting it means you stop making up your own structure and instead model everything against CSDM's domains, so the data is usable by more than just the person who built it.
commonMistakes: Describing CSDM as a module, plugin, or setting rather than a reference framework
Missing the cross-module inconsistency problem (ITSM vs. ITOM vs. SPM expecting different shapes)
Missing the cross-customer problem of re-deriving structure on every engagement
Assuming adopting CSDM is purely documentation with no real modeling change
keyPoints: CSDM is a reference framework/documented structure, not a feature or setting
It solves real inconsistency within one instance across modules
It solves real re-derivation waste across different implementations/customers
Adopting it changes how an implementer models CIs, applications, and services going forward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly characterizes CSDM as a reference framework, not a feature
Explains the real cross-module and cross-customer cost it solves
Explains what concretely changes about data modeling after adoption
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Identification Rules vs. Reconciliation Rules
questions.prompt: Explain the precise difference between an Identification Rule and a Reconciliation Rule in the CMDB, using independent and dependent identifiers in your explanation. Then explain why a server's Identification Rule can be working correctly while its Reconciliation Rule still produces wrong data on that same CI.
questions.modelAnswer: An Identification Rule decides whether two incoming records describe the same real-world asset, using a per-CI-class definition built from an independent identifier (reliable on its own, like a hardware serial number) and dependent identifiers (reliable only in combination, like Host Name plus Domain). A Reconciliation Rule solves a different problem entirely: once two sources are confirmed to be the same CI, it decides which source's value wins when they disagree on a specific field, using a designated authoritative source per field rather than a 'most recent write wins' default. Because these rules answer different questions, a server's Identification Rule can correctly recognize that Discovery's record and a manual import both describe the same machine — merging them onto one CI — while the Reconciliation Rule still lets a stale manual-import value for, say, OS version silently overwrite a correct, freshly-discovered value, because no authoritative source was designated for that field. One rule type cannot substitute for the other.
questions.professionalAnswer: Identification answers 'is this the same thing,' Reconciliation answers 'whose value do I trust when they disagree' — two completely separate jobs. Identification uses attributes like a serial number alone, or hostname plus domain together, to merge records onto one CI correctly. Reconciliation then decides, field by field, which source gets to win when Discovery and a manual import disagree. So yes, you can have perfectly correct merging — one CI, not two — and still have bad data on that CI, because nobody told the platform which source should be trusted for OS version specifically. That's exactly why both rules have to be configured, and why fixing duplicates doesn't automatically fix data correctness.
commonMistakes: Treating Identification and Reconciliation as the same mechanism or interchangeable
Not distinguishing independent identifiers from dependent identifiers
Assuming correct identification guarantees correct field-level data
Defaulting to 'most recent write wins' as an acceptable reconciliation strategy
keyPoints: Identification Rules decide whether two records are the same CI
Reconciliation Rules decide which source's value wins per field when sources disagree
Independent identifiers work alone; dependent identifiers only work in combination
Correct identification with no/bad reconciliation still produces wrong field data on a correctly-merged CI

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes Identification from Reconciliation Rules
Correctly uses independent vs. dependent identifiers
Explains why correct identification doesn't guarantee correct reconciliation
Clear, precise explanation

questions.title: Where the Password Actually Lives in SAML-Based SSO
questions.prompt: Walk through the SAML login flow between ServiceNow (the Service Provider) and an external Identity Provider step by step. At exactly which step does the user's password exist, and at exactly which step does ServiceNow cryptographically verify the assertion, and against what stored record?
questions.modelAnswer: The flow runs: the user navigates to the ServiceNow instance; ServiceNow redirects the browser to the configured Identity Provider's SSO endpoint; the user authenticates directly at the IdP with whatever credentials and MFA it enforces; the IdP builds a signed SAML assertion confirming the user's identity; the browser carries that signed assertion back to ServiceNow; ServiceNow validates the assertion's signature; and finally ServiceNow logs the user in, handing off to the existing sys_user record, roles, and groups. The password exists only at step three, entirely inside the IdP — ServiceNow is never handed it at any point. ServiceNow's verification happens at the signature-validation step, and it checks that signature against the IdP's signing certificate stored in the instance's Multi-Provider SSO configuration record, the same record that also holds the entity ID and SSO endpoint URL establishing the trust relationship in the first place.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk it step by step because that's exactly how you troubleshoot it too. User hits the instance, gets bounced to the IdP, authenticates there — password and MFA both live entirely at that step, ServiceNow never sees them. The IdP signs an assertion and hands it back through the browser, and ServiceNow's job is just to verify that signature against the certificate it has on file in the Multi-Provider SSO config record. If that checks out, the user's existing sys_user record and roles take over like normal. So the real answer to 'where's the password' is: nowhere near ServiceNow, ever — and the real answer to 'where's the verification' is: a signature check against a stored certificate, not a password check at all.
commonMistakes: Assuming ServiceNow receives or checks the user's password at some point in the flow
Confusing the signature-verification step with a generic 'ServiceNow trusts the IdP' hand-wave
Not naming the Multi-Provider SSO configuration record as what the signature is actually checked against
Missing that the entity ID and SSO endpoint URL are also part of establishing the trust relationship
keyPoints: The password exists only at the IdP authentication step, never at ServiceNow
ServiceNow verifies a signed assertion's signature, not a password
That verification checks against the IdP signing certificate in the Multi-Provider SSO configuration record
After verification, the existing sys_user record, roles, and groups take over as normal

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly walks through the full SAML login flow in order
Correctly identifies exactly where the password exists
Correctly identifies the signature-verification step and what it checks against
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Domain-Separated vs. Domain-Extendable Data
questions.prompt: Explain the concrete behavioral difference between data marked domain-separated and data marked domain-extendable in a ServiceNow instance with Domain Separation enabled. Give a realistic example of a Business Rule or Script Include where getting this choice wrong causes either a data leak between domains or a loss of centralized management.
questions.modelAnswer: Domain-separated data is visible only within its own domain and to domains above it in the hierarchy — a sibling domain can never see it, by design. Domain-extendable data is visible and editable from the top/primary domain down into any subordinate domain, which lets an MSP or parent-company admin team manage shared configuration centrally across every client or subsidiary. Getting this wrong cuts both ways: if a Script Include that should remain domain-extendable (a shared utility the MSP needs to patch centrally) is instead marked domain-separated, the MSP admin loses the ability to manage it from the top domain, and now has to duplicate fixes into every subordinate domain separately. The more dangerous direction is the reverse: if a Business Rule or table holding Client X's sensitive data is accidentally left domain-extendable when it should be domain-separated, Client Y's domain — or any domain above Client X's — may be able to see or touch data that was supposed to be airtight, which is exactly the kind of leak Domain Separation exists to prevent.
questions.professionalAnswer: Domain-separated means locked to its own domain and anything above it — a sibling domain never sees it. Domain-extendable means the top domain can see and edit it anywhere underneath, which is what lets a parent or MSP manage shared config centrally. The real danger is in the mislabeling: mark something domain-separated that was supposed to be centrally managed, and now the MSP is stuck patching five client domains by hand instead of one place. Mark something domain-extendable that was supposed to be airtight between clients, and you've got an actual data leak — one client's incidents visible somewhere they never should have been. Both mistakes are real, and they're exactly why every Business Rule and Script Include on a domain-separated instance has to be reasoned about explicitly rather than left to its default.
commonMistakes: Describing domain-separated and domain-extendable without the concrete visibility/editability difference
Only naming the data-leak direction and missing the lost-centralized-management direction
Assuming this choice is a one-time setup detail rather than something every new customization must consider
Testing only from the top domain, which sees everything, and missing subordinate-domain behavior
keyPoints: Domain-separated: visible only to its own domain and domains above it
Domain-extendable: visible/editable from the top domain down into subordinate domains
Mislabeling toward domain-separated loses centralized management
Mislabeling toward domain-extendable risks a real cross-domain data leak

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the behavioral difference between the two
Gives a realistic, concrete example of getting it wrong in each direction
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: The Business Rule Execution Sequence, End to End
questions.prompt: State the complete, fixed sequence a single record save goes through across Before, After, and Async Business Rules, including where the database write itself occurs and where Display Business Rules sit relative to all of it. Then explain what the numeric order field actually breaks ties on.
questions.modelAnswer: The fixed sequence is: every applicable Before Business Rule runs, in order; then the database write itself occurs; then every applicable After Business Rule runs, in order; then any applicable Async Business Rules are queued to run later in the background, outside the main save transaction. Display Business Rules sit entirely outside this chain — they run on form load, not on save, so they never appear in this sequence at all. The order field is purely a tiebreaker among rules that share the same timing (Before, After, or Async) on the same table: when two Before rules both apply to the same save, the lower order value runs first, in full, before the next one starts. Order has no effect across different timings — it never makes an After rule run before a Before rule; it only decides sequencing within one timing group.
questions.professionalAnswer: The sequence is fixed and worth knowing cold: Before rules in order, then the actual write to the database, then After rules in order, then Async rules get queued for later. Display rules are a separate thing entirely — they fire on form load, not save, so they're not part of this chain at all. The order field only matters as a tiebreaker inside one timing bucket — two Before rules on the same table, lower order runs first. It's not a global priority number across the whole sequence; a Before rule with order 900 still runs before every After rule, no matter what order value that After rule has.
commonMistakes: Omitting the Async queuing step or describing it as running synchronously
Placing Display Business Rules inside the save sequence instead of correctly excluding them
Treating the order field as a global priority across Before/After/Async rather than a same-timing tiebreaker
Getting the Before-write-After sequence out of order
keyPoints: Sequence: Before rules (in order) -> database write -> After rules (in order) -> Async rules queued
Display Business Rules run on form load, entirely outside this save sequence
The order field only breaks ties among rules sharing the same timing on the same table
Order never lets a later timing group run before an earlier one

evaluationCriteria.criterion: States the complete, correctly-ordered sequence
Correctly places Display Business Rules outside the sequence
Correctly explains what the order field actually breaks ties on
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Why Cross-Scope Access Is Closed by Default
questions.prompt: Explain why a Script Include inside one scoped application cannot be called from another scope by default, and name the two real mechanisms that open that access deliberately. Why does ServiceNow's documentation recommend Cross-Scope Access Control over setting "Accessible from" to "All application scopes" for anything beyond a generic utility?
questions.modelAnswer: Scope isolates both naming and access by default: ServiceNow assumes isolation unless a developer explicitly opens a door, rather than assuming openness unless someone locks one, which makes the security posture of any scoped application predictable without having to hunt for hidden, unintended access paths. Two real mechanisms open that door deliberately. First, a Script Include's "Accessible from" field can be flipped from the default "This application scope only" to "All application scopes," which is a broad, blanket grant to every scope on the instance with no record of who actually uses it or why. Second, a Cross-Scope Access Control record (sys_scope_privilege) grants one specific calling scope access to one specific target — a table, API, or Script Include — in another scope, and nothing broader. ServiceNow recommends the targeted mechanism for anything beyond a generic, non-sensitive utility because it's auditable and least-privilege: an instance reviewer can see exactly which scope was granted access to exactly what and why, instead of discovering a Script Include was quietly opened to the entire instance with no trace of intent.
questions.professionalAnswer: The default is closed, not open, on purpose — nobody auditing an instance should have to go hunting for access that was never deliberately granted. Opening it up has two real paths: flip 'Accessible from' to all scopes, which is a blunt, instance-wide grant with zero record of who's actually using it, or create a Cross-Scope Access Control record that names exactly which scope gets exactly which target. ServiceNow pushes you toward the second option for anything real because it's auditable — someone reviewing the instance later can see precisely what was granted and to whom, instead of finding a wide-open door nobody remembers opening.
commonMistakes: Assuming scope isolation is only about naming collisions, not access control
Treating the two mechanisms as interchangeable rather than appropriate for different risk levels
Not naming sys_scope_privilege as the actual table backing Cross-Scope Access Control
Missing the audit/least-privilege justification for preferring the targeted mechanism
keyPoints: Scope access is closed by default, deliberately, for predictable security review
"Accessible from: All application scopes" is a broad, untargeted grant
Cross-Scope Access Control (sys_scope_privilege) grants one scope access to one specific target
The targeted mechanism is preferred for anything beyond a generic utility because it's auditable and least-privilege

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why cross-scope access is closed by default
Correctly names and describes both mechanisms
Explains the audit/least-privilege reasoning for preferring Cross-Scope Access Control
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Why SLA Duration Math Is Schedule-Aware, Not Flat Wall-Clock Time
questions.prompt: A 4-hour Priority-3 SLA Definition references the "8-5 Weekdays" schedule and starts at 4:00 PM on a Friday. Explain precisely when it breaches in real wall-clock time, and why attaching no schedule at all to that same SLA Definition would be a serious implementation error, even though it would be the "simpler" configuration.
questions.modelAnswer: With the 8-5 Weekdays schedule attached, the SLA clock only accumulates time while that schedule is open. Starting at 4:00 PM Friday, it accrues one hour before the schedule closes for the weekend at 5:00 PM, then sits paused through Friday evening, all of Saturday, and all of Sunday, resuming Monday at 8:00 AM with 3 hours remaining — so it breaches at 11:00 AM Monday, not at 8:00 PM Friday. Attaching no schedule at all would make the SLA run 24/7, so the same 4-hour target would breach at 8:00 PM Friday instead — a dramatically different, and wrong, result for a Priority-3 expectation that should only count business hours. That's a serious implementation error specifically because it's silent: the SLA Definition still looks fully configured and will quietly generate a wave of false breaches every time a ticket is opened late in the week, with nothing in the configuration itself flagging that the duration math means something completely different than the business intended.
questions.professionalAnswer: Business-hours math, not a flat countdown — that's the whole point of attaching a schedule. Starting at 4 PM Friday against 8-5 Weekdays, you get one hour of accrual before the weekend closes it down, then it sits frozen until Monday morning and breaches around 11 AM Monday with the remaining three hours used up. Skip the schedule and it's 24/7 math instead, breaching Friday night — which might be fine for a true round-the-clock Priority 1, but it's wrong for a Priority 3 that was only ever supposed to count business hours. The reason this is a serious error and not just a minor tuning issue is that it's invisible in the configuration itself — the SLA Definition looks complete, it just silently measures the wrong thing, generating false breaches nobody notices until someone asks why Priority 3 breach rates look so bad.
commonMistakes: Calculating the breach time as flat 24/7 math even though a schedule is attached
Not recognizing that 'no schedule' means 24/7 by default, not 'no SLA'
Treating the choice of schedule as a minor detail rather than something that changes the real meaning of the duration
Failing to explain why this error is silent rather than something that throws an obvious configuration error
keyPoints: A schedule-aware SLA only accrues time while the referenced schedule is open
The example breaches around 11 AM the following Monday, not Friday night
No schedule attached means 24/7 duration math by default
Using the wrong schedule (or none) is a silent error that produces false breaches, not an obvious configuration failure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly calculates the schedule-aware breach time
Correctly explains the 24/7-default consequence of no schedule
Explains why this is a serious, silent implementation error
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Horizontal Discovery vs. Vertical Discovery
questions.prompt: An incident responder needs a precise, end-to-end dependency map for one business-critical application during an outage, tracing it from the web tier down to the storage array underneath its database. Explain why Horizontal Discovery alone would not give them this, what Vertical Discovery does differently, and why a mature CMDB program runs both rather than choosing one.
questions.modelAnswer: Horizontal Discovery performs a broad sweep across many infrastructure types in a scanned range — servers, network devices, databases — to build general CMDB coverage, but it has no concept of any one application's specific dependency chain; it classifies what exists without tracing how any of it connects to any other piece for a given service. That leaves exactly the gap an incident responder cares about during an outage: knowing what infrastructure exists broadly doesn't tell you what this one critical application actually depends on, end to end. Vertical Discovery solves that different problem by going deep on one specific application, tracing its full chain — web server to load balancer to application server to database to the storage array beneath it — closely related to Service Mapping. A mature CMDB program runs both because they answer different real questions: Horizontal for 'what do we have, broadly,' Vertical for 'what does this one business-critical service actually depend on, precisely' — and an incident responder needs the second, not the first.
questions.professionalAnswer: Horizontal Discovery is a wide net — it's great for knowing what infrastructure exists across an environment, but it was never built to trace one service's specific dependency chain. Vertical Discovery is the opposite: it goes deep on exactly one application, tracing it tier by tier down to the storage underneath its database, which is exactly what an incident responder needs when something's down and they need to know what to check first. A program that only runs Horizontal has great general coverage and no precise map for the services that actually matter most during an outage. A program that only runs Vertical has great maps for a handful of critical apps and no general awareness of everything else. Real programs run both because they're answering genuinely different questions.
commonMistakes: Assuming Horizontal Discovery produces dependency chains as a side effect of broad scanning
Confusing Vertical Discovery with a narrower version of the same horizontal sweep
Not connecting Vertical Discovery to Service Mapping explicitly
Picking one discovery mode as categorically 'better' instead of recognizing they solve different problems
keyPoints: Horizontal Discovery builds broad, general infrastructure coverage without tracing dependency chains
Vertical Discovery traces one specific service's full dependency chain, closely tied to Service Mapping
An incident responder needs the precise, per-service map Vertical Discovery provides
Mature programs run both because they answer different real questions

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why Horizontal Discovery alone is insufficient here
Correctly explains what Vertical Discovery does differently
Explains why both are run together rather than choosing one
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Fixing an N+1 GlideRecord Query Pattern
questions.prompt: You inherit a scheduled script that loops over every active cmn_department record and, inside that loop, runs a fresh GlideRecord query against the incident table to count open incidents for that department. There are 400 departments. Rewrite this so it executes as a single query against incident and tallies counts per department in memory, and explain why your version scales independently of the number of departments.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd pull this inside out: query incident once for everything active, tally counts into a plain object keyed by department sys_id while I loop through, then query departments separately and just look up each one's count from the map. That's two queries flat, regardless of whether there are 400 departments or 4,000 — the original scales its query count with department count, mine doesn't scale at all on that axis. The underlying issue is recognizing the N+1 shape: one query to get N rows, plus N more queries triggered inside the loop over those rows.
commonMistakes: Optimizing the inner query (e.g. adding setLimit) instead of eliminating it
Forgetting to filter the single incident query to active=true, changing the semantics
Using getRowCount() per department instead of aggregating into a map
Not explaining why the rewrite's query count is independent of department count
keyPoints: The original is a classic N+1 pattern: 1 query to get departments, N more inside the loop
The fix is one query against incident, with counting done in memory via a JS object
Total query count becomes constant (2), independent of the number of departments
This generalizes to any 'query inside a loop over another query's results' pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly rewrites the pattern as a single query plus in-memory tally
Resulting code is correct and preserves the active=true filter
Clearly explains why query count is now independent of department count
Code is clean and readable

questions.title: Replacing a Counting Loop With GlideAggregate
questions.prompt: A dashboard widget currently opens a GlideRecord against incident filtered to active=true and priority=1, loops through every row incrementing a counter, and discards each record after counting it. Rewrite this using the correct API for a pure count, and explain specifically why your version never pulls full row data from the database at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: Swap GlideRecord for GlideAggregate and add the COUNT aggregate instead of looping. The real difference is where the counting happens: GlideAggregate pushes the count down to the database itself, which returns one number, while the GlideRecord version pulls back every single matching row's full data and only then counts them one by one in the script, throwing away everything it just fetched. Same filters, completely different amount of work on both the database and the app server.
commonMistakes: Keeping the GlideRecord loop and only adding setLimit, which doesn't eliminate full-row retrieval
Forgetting addAggregate('COUNT') before calling query()
Reading the result without calling ga.next() first
Not explaining that the database itself performs the count, rather than the script counting rows it fetched
keyPoints: GlideAggregate is the correct API for COUNT/SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX, grouped or ungrouped
The aggregate is computed at the database level, returning one value
No full row data crosses back to the script at all
getAggregate('COUNT') after ga.next() retrieves the computed value

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly rewrites the counting logic using GlideAggregate

questions.title: Building a Client-Callable Script Include for GlideAjax
questions.prompt: Write a Script Include named VendorContractLookup that a client script will call via GlideAjax to check, given a vendor's sys_id passed as a parameter, whether that vendor's contract is currently active. Include a private helper method the client must never be able to reach directly, and name every platform-level setting that has to be correct, beyond the script itself, for the call to actually work.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd extend AbstractAjaxProcessor, write a public method with a plain name for the client to call, read the vendor's sys_id with getParameter, and push the actual GlideRecord lookup into a private helper prefixed with an underscore. The two things that have to be true outside the code itself: Client callable has to be checked on the Script Include record — it's off by default for a reason — and the class has to extend AbstractAjaxProcessor, because that's the only thing that actually wires it into GlideAjax's plumbing. The underscore on the helper isn't decoration — the platform itself refuses to let the client reach a method named that way, callable flag or not.

Naming the helper without a leading underscore, accidentally exposing it to the client
Not mentioning the 'Client callable' checkbox as a required, non-default platform setting
Returning a raw boolean instead of a string, which can behave unexpectedly across the GlideAjax client boundary

questions.title: Writing a Class-Based Script Include With the Standard Pattern
questions.prompt: Write a class-based Script Include named ChangeRiskCalculator using the Class.create() pattern, with an initialize() constructor that sets a default risk threshold, and a method isHighRisk(gr) that compares a Change Request's calculated risk field against that threshold. Include the required trailing property every class-based Script Include needs, and explain what silently breaks if that property is left out of sync after a rename.
questions.professionalAnswer: Standard shape: Class.create() for the constructor, a prototype object with initialize() setting the default threshold, the real method, and a trailing type string matching the class name exactly. That type property isn't just style — ServiceNow's own internal reflection reads it to know what class it's actually looking at, which matters for things like error logging. If you rename the class but forget to update that string, nothing throws an error — JavaScript doesn't care — but anything that relies on reading type to identify the object correctly now reports the stale old name, and that's a bug that's genuinely easy to miss during a rename because it never surfaces as a visible failure.

Using Object.extendsObject when a plain Class.create() pattern (no base class) is all that's needed
Putting the threshold comparison logic inside initialize() instead of in isHighRisk()
Not explaining that a stale type string causes a silent, non-crashing bug rather than an obvious error

initialize() is the constructor, running immediately at instantiation
type must be a string exactly matching the class name, used by the platform's internal reflection
A stale type string after a rename causes a silent misidentification bug, not a runtime error

Includes a correct type property
Correctly explains the consequence of a stale type after a rename

questions.title: Configuring OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials for an Unattended Nightly Sync
questions.prompt: A nightly scheduled job pulls pricing data from a partner's REST API with no human user involved. Describe, concretely, the OAuth Entity record and OAuth Entity Profile configuration you would set up, which grant type you'd select and why, and exactly what ServiceNow handles automatically for you once that profile is attached to the REST Message's Authentication Profile.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd first create an OAuth Entity record holding the real connection details for the partner system: the client ID, the client secret, and the token endpoint URL the partner expects token requests to hit. On top of that, I'd create an OAuth Entity Profile pointing at that OAuth Entity record, and set its grant type to Client Credentials — the correct choice here because the integration authenticates purely as itself, with no human user's authorization involved at any point, which is exactly the Client Credentials use case (as opposed to Authorization Code, which requires a human consent step). Finally, I'd attach that OAuth Entity Profile to the REST Message's Authentication Profile. Once that's wired up, ServiceNow automatically requests an access token the first time it's needed, caches it for reuse across subsequent nightly runs, and silently requests a fresh token when the cached one expires or is rejected — the script itself never has to track token expiry, catch 401s, or re-authenticate manually.
questions.professionalAnswer: Set up the OAuth Entity record first with the client ID, secret, and token endpoint the partner gave us, then an OAuth Entity Profile on top pointing at that record with Client Credentials as the grant type — no human in the loop, so that's the right choice over Authorization Code. Attach the profile to the REST Message's Authentication Profile and that's it from a code perspective. The real win is that ServiceNow now owns the entire token lifecycle: first request fetches a token, it gets cached and reused, and a fresh one gets pulled automatically when it expires — none of that logic has to live in my scheduled script.

Describing token management as something the script has to implement manually
Confusing the OAuth Entity record (connection details) with the OAuth Entity Profile (grant type selection)
Forgetting to connect the profile to the REST Message's Authentication Profile
keyPoints: OAuth Entity record holds client ID, client secret, and the token endpoint URL
OAuth Entity Profile selects the grant type and points at the OAuth Entity record
Client Credentials grant fits here because no human user's authorization is involved
ServiceNow automatically requests, caches, and refreshes the token once configured

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the OAuth Entity record and OAuth Entity Profile setup
Correctly selects and justifies Client Credentials grant

questions.title: Implementing Exponential Backoff for a Flaky Partner API
questions.prompt: A REST Message call to a partner API occasionally returns a 503 under load. Write server-side script that retries the call up to 4 times using exponential backoff starting at 1 second, and explain specifically why retrying immediately in a tight loop would make the partner's overload worse rather than better.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd wrap the REST Message call in a loop that doubles its wait time on each failed attempt — 1, 2, 4, 8 seconds — using gs.sleep() between tries, and stop retrying once it either succeeds or hits the retry cap. The reason a tight, immediate retry loop backfires is pretty intuitive once you say it out loud: if the partner system is already overloaded, every caller immediately hammering it again the instant a request fails just adds to the exact load that caused the problem. Backoff does two things: it gives the system room to actually recover, and it naturally desynchronizes everyone's retries instead of having them all pile back on at once.

Forgetting to cap the number of retries, risking an effectively infinite retry loop
Not explaining the thundering-herd effect of immediate retries from many callers
Treating this as safe to retry without first confirming the operation is idempotent
keyPoints: Exponential backoff doubles the wait between retries (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s...)
gs.sleep(ms) is the real server-side API used to implement the wait
Immediate, tight-loop retries add to the exact load causing the overload
Backoff also naturally spreads out retries from many simultaneous callers

questions.title: Building a Custom Reusable Flow Designer Action
questions.prompt: Three different flows (Incident, Change, and a Service Catalog fulfillment flow) each need to calculate an SLA due date from a priority level and a start timestamp. Describe the Inputs, internal steps, and Outputs you would define for a custom Action Designer action that centralizes this logic, and explain concretely what breaks down operationally if this logic is instead copy-pasted into all three flows.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd build one custom action in Action Designer, something like 'Calculate SLA Due Date.' Its Inputs would be a priority level and a start timestamp. Its internal steps would run the actual business logic once — mapping priority to a response-window duration and computing the resulting due date/time, using whatever combination of built-in actions and a scripting step the calculation requires. Its Output would be the calculated due date, exposed as a data pill the calling flow consumes exactly like any built-in action's output. Any of the three flows that needs an SLA due date calls this one action instead of re-implementing the date math independently. If instead each flow copy-pasted its own version of this logic, a future change to the business rule (say, priority definitions change, or a new priority tier is added) means finding and correctly re-editing the logic in three separate places, and missing even one is exactly how the three flows quietly drift out of sync with each other — one flow computing a different due date than the other two for the same inputs, with no single obvious place to look when that discrepancy eventually gets noticed.
questions.professionalAnswer: One custom action, built once in Action Designer: priority level and start timestamp as Inputs, the actual priority-to-duration mapping and date math as the internal steps, and the resulting due date as the Output every calling flow consumes as a normal data pill. The real cost of skipping this and copy-pasting the same logic into Incident, Change, and the catalog fulfillment flow shows up the first time the business rule changes — now there are three places to find and fix instead of one, and the realistic outcome of that is someone updates two of the three and the third quietly keeps computing a different due date until somebody notices the inconsistency the hard way.

Missing that the Output becomes a data pill consumed identically to a built-in action's output
Only describing the maintenance cost abstractly instead of naming the concrete drift-between-flows failure
Suggesting each flow should keep its own copy 'for flexibility' without acknowledging the real cost

Internal steps: the priority-to-duration mapping and date math, built once
Output: the calculated due date, consumed as a normal data pill by any calling flow
Copy-pasted logic across flows drifts out of sync the first time the business rule changes

Correctly explains how the action is consumed by calling flows

questions.title: Writing a Fast, Correct ACL Script for Group-Scoped Access
questions.prompt: Write the script for an ACL that should grant write access to a record only to members of the group referenced in that record's assignment_group field. Use the correct, standard ServiceNow pattern rather than issuing a fresh GlideRecord query against sys_user_grmember, and explain precisely why the query-based version is a real, measurable performance risk at instance scale when it's repeated across every record, every field, every page load.
questions.modelAnswer:
answer = gs.getUser().isMemberOf(current.assignment_group);

gs.getUser() returns the current transaction's GlideUser object, already loaded once per transaction with the user's roles and group memberships; isMemberOf() answers the group-membership question directly from that already-loaded data, with no fresh database round trip. The query-based alternative (a GlideRecord against sys_user_grmember filtered to the current user and the group) issues a real database query every single time the ACL runs, and an ACL script doesn't run once per transaction — it runs on every access attempt to the record or field it governs: every form load, every list view including that field, every Table API call, every report. A 50-millisecond query-based check multiplied across every user, every record, every field reference, all day, becomes a measurable, avoidable instance-wide performance cost, which is exactly why it's one of the most common, least obvious causes of a slow instance that nobody thinks to check first.
questions.professionalAnswer: answer = gs.getUser().isMemberOf(current.assignment_group) — one line, no query, because gs.getUser() already has the current user's group memberships loaded for the transaction. The reason I'd never write a fresh GlideRecord query against sys_user_grmember here isn't just style — ACL scripts run on every access attempt to whatever they govern, not once per transaction. A query that adds even 50 milliseconds gets multiplied across every user, every record, every field reference, all day long, and that adds up to a real, instance-wide performance problem that's genuinely easy to miss because no single request looks slow on its own.
commonMistakes: Writing a fresh GlideRecord query against sys_user_grmember instead of using isMemberOf()
Not recognizing that ACL scripts run on every access attempt, not once per transaction
Treating a 50ms delay in an ACL script as equivalent in impact to the same delay in a scheduled job
Hardcoding a group sys_id instead of reading it from current.assignment_group
keyPoints: gs.getUser().isMemberOf() answers group membership without a fresh query
ACL scripts run on every single access attempt to the governed record/field
A small per-check delay compounds into a real, instance-wide performance cost
Prefer data already on current or the cached GlideUser over querying elsewhere

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses gs.getUser().isMemberOf() instead of a fresh query
Code correctly references current.assignment_group
Clearly explains why ACL script performance compounds instance-wide
Clear, accurate overall answer

questions.title: Granting Targeted Cross-Scope Access Instead of Opening a Script Include Broadly
questions.prompt: A Script Include inside your core ITSM scoped application, x_acme_itsm, needs to be called by exactly one other scoped application, x_acme_fieldservice, and by nothing else on the instance. Describe the specific mechanism you'd configure to grant that access, why you would not simply set the Script Include's "Accessible from" field to "All application scopes," and what an auditor reviewing the instance would be able to see as a result of your choice.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd create a Cross-Scope Access Control record (sys_scope_privilege) that names x_acme_fieldservice as the calling scope and the specific Script Include in x_acme_itsm as the target, and nothing broader. I would not set "Accessible from" to "All application scopes" because that opens the Script Include to every scope on the instance — Global and every other scoped application, present and future — with no record anywhere of which scope actually needs it or why; it's the mechanism of last resort for genuinely generic, non-sensitive utilities, not for a core ITSM Script Include with real business logic behind it. With a targeted Cross-Scope Access Control record instead, an auditor reviewing the instance can see exactly one grant: x_acme_fieldservice is permitted to call this one specific Script Include in x_acme_itsm, and nothing else in that scope is reachable from outside it. That's the entire point of the least-privilege, auditable mechanism — the grant is visible, specific, and traceable to a real intentional decision, rather than discovered as an unexplained, instance-wide opening.
questions.professionalAnswer: A Cross-Scope Access Control record naming x_acme_fieldservice as the caller and this one Script Include as the target — nothing wider. I'd stay away from flipping Accessible from to all scopes because that's a blanket grant to literally everything on the instance, present and future, with zero record of intent behind it; that's fine for a generic date formatter, not for a core ITSM Script Include. The payoff of doing it the targeted way is exactly what an auditor would see: one specific, named grant, and everything else in x_acme_itsm still closed to outside scopes by default.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to 'Accessible from: All application scopes' for convenience
Not naming sys_scope_privilege as the specific mechanism/table involved
Describing the grant as broader than the one named calling scope
Missing the auditability argument for why the targeted mechanism is preferred
keyPoints: Cross-Scope Access Control (sys_scope_privilege) grants one named scope access to one named target
"All application scopes" is a broad, untargeted, unaudited grant to the entire instance
The targeted mechanism is the least-privilege, auditable choice for real business logic
An auditor sees exactly one named, intentional grant rather than a wide-open door

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly specifies a Cross-Scope Access Control record naming the specific scope and target
Correctly explains why 'All application scopes' is the wrong choice here
Correctly explains what an auditor would see as a result
Clear, accurate overall answer

questions.title: Fixing a Recursive Business Rule
questions.prompt: A Business Rule named "Calculate Priority Score" runs after insert/update on incident, computes a score, and saves it back with current.update(). Debug output shows it firing six times for a single form save, with execution durations shrinking toward zero each time. Rewrite the script with the two specific changes that fix this, and explain what the shrinking-duration pattern in the debug output was actually telling you about the script's behavior before your fix.
questions.professionalAnswer: Two changes fix it: check whether the new score actually differs from the stored one before doing anything, and call current.setWorkflow(false) right before the update so this particular save doesn't re-fire business rules on incident at all. The shrinking durations in the debug panel were the real tell — that's not six separate slow executions, that's one business rule's own save re-triggering itself, recalculating a converging value each time, until the value stops changing and the platform's recursion cap finally ends it. Once you see that shape — same rule, repeating, durations trending toward zero — it's always this exact pattern.

ServiceNow caps recursion depth, which is why the loop eventually stops on its own, inefficiently

questions.title: Writing a Server-Side ATF Test That Validates a Script Include's Return Value
questions.prompt: Describe how you would structure a server-side ATF Test (not a UI Test) to validate that a Script Include method named calculateRiskScore returns the expected numeric value for a known Change Request input, and explain concretely why a server-side Test here would catch a regression in that method that a UI Test on the Change form might completely miss.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd build a server-side Test whose Test Step calls the Script Include's calculateRiskScore method directly, with a known input (either a specific GlideRecord set up by an earlier step, or representative field values), and asserts that the returned value matches the expected result for that input — no form is opened, filled in, or submitted anywhere in the Test. The reason this catches a regression a UI Test might miss is that the two Tests exercise genuinely different layers: a UI Test only confirms what a user sees and experiences on the form — the right field visible, the right value displayed — and it's entirely possible for a UI Policy or client-side validation on that form to mask or compensate for a wrong value coming back from calculateRiskScore, so the form still 'looks right' while the underlying logic is actually broken. A server-side Test checks the Script Include's contract directly, independent of whatever form eventually calls it, so a change that silently breaks calculateRiskScore's return value for a given input is caught immediately, with no dependency on the form's own behavior accidentally hiding the bug.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write a Test Step that calls calculateRiskScore directly with a known input and asserts the return value matches what's expected — completely bypassing the Change form. The reason that catches something a UI Test could miss is that a UI Test only proves the form behaves right; it doesn't prove the logic behind it is right, because a UI Policy or some client-side validation on that same form could quietly mask a wrong value coming back from the Script Include. Testing the method's contract directly means a regression in the actual logic gets caught immediately, regardless of whether the form happens to look fine on top of it.

Not explaining the specific failure mode where a UI Policy masks a wrong underlying value
Treating server-side and UI Tests as redundant rather than catching genuinely different bug categories
Omitting the assertion step (checking the actual return value against the expected one)

It asserts the returned value against a known expected result for a known input

questions.title: Calling GlideAjax From a Client Script to Validate a Field Before Submit
questions.prompt: Write an onSubmit client script that calls the VendorContractLookup Script Include from question 013 via GlideAjax, passing the selected vendor's sys_id, and blocks form submission with a clear message if the contract is not active. Explain why this check has to happen through GlideAjax rather than a direct GlideRecord query written into the client script itself.

questions.title: Diagnosing a Recursive Business Rule From Its Debug Signature
questions.prompt: A single agent save produces six consecutive debug-panel entries for the same Business Rule, with durations of 14ms, 14ms, 14ms, 11ms, 9ms, 0ms. Explain what this specific pattern tells you about the underlying cause before you've even opened the script, and what you would look for inside the script to confirm your suspicion.
questions.modelAnswer: The signature — the same Business Rule name repeated several times for one user action, with durations trending down toward zero — is the classic shape of a recursive trigger converging toward a stable value, not six independent slow executions. Each run is individually fast, which is exactly why this kind of problem often goes unnoticed in a casual duration-only scan; what gives it away is the repeat count and the converging trend, not any single run looking alarming. questions.professionalAnswer: That exact shape — same rule name, several entries, durations shrinking toward zero — isn't six slow runs, it's one rule re-triggering itself and converging to a stop. questions.title: Semaphore Exhaustion Disguised as a Slow Script
questions.prompt: A scheduled job that normally completes in under a second is now taking eight seconds end to end, but when you isolate and time the script itself, it still finishes in well under a second. Explain what's actually happening, why optimizing the script further would be the wrong fix, and what you would check instead to confirm the real cause.
questions.modelAnswer: The eight-second wall-clock time almost certainly includes real queue time, not execution time: the job's category of work (background/scheduled) is competing for a limited, per-node semaphore pool, and when every slot in that pool is currently busy with other work, a new job of the same type has to wait its turn before it even starts running. From the outside, that wait looks identical to ordinary slowness — 'this job took eight seconds' — but the script itself, once it finally gets a slot, still only takes under a second, which is exactly the clue that something upstream of execution is the real bottleneck. Optimizing the script further would be the wrong fix because the script was never the slow part; shaving its execution time from under a second to even less time does nothing to shorten how long it has to wait in a saturated queue. What I'd check instead is the node's semaphore/node-usage data to see whether the relevant category's pool is saturated, and if so, investigate what's actually filling that pool — likely another job or a burst of jobs in the same category competing for the same limited slots.
questions.professionalAnswer: That gap between an eight-second wall-clock time and a sub-second actual execution time is the real tell — this job spent most of its time waiting for a semaphore slot, not running. Optimizing the script wouldn't help because the script was never the problem; it's already fast. I'd go look at semaphore and node usage directly to confirm the relevant pool was saturated at that time, and then figure out what else was piling into that same category of work and crowding it out.

Proposing script-level optimizations as the fix without checking for queue delay first
Not distinguishing wall-clock time from actual execution time as separate diagnostic signals
Failing to name semaphore/node usage data as the specific thing to check

Semaphore exhaustion makes a fast script look slow from the outside
Optimizing an already-fast script does nothing to shorten queue wait time
Semaphore and node usage data is the correct place to confirm pool saturation

Correctly explains why script optimization would not help

Clear, accurate overall reasoning

questions.title: Diagnosing a GlideRecord-in-a-Loop Problem From the Slow Request Log
questions.prompt: The Slow Request Log flags a transaction whose total time is dominated by hundreds of short database query entries rather than one long-running query. Explain what pattern in that time breakdown points specifically to an N+1 GlideRecord problem rather than one genuinely slow query, and how you would confirm it by reading the script the transaction actually ran.
questions.modelAnswer: A single genuinely slow query shows up as one line item with a long individual duration — the signature of a bad execution plan, a missing index, or an unusually expensive filter. Hundreds of short query entries, each individually fast but numerous enough to dominate the total transaction time, is the opposite signature: it points to the same query (or a structurally similar one) being issued repeatedly, once per iteration of some outer loop, which is exactly the N+1 pattern — one query to fetch N rows, plus N more queries triggered inside a loop over those rows. To confirm it, I'd read the actual script behind the transaction looking for a GlideRecord query (or .next() loop) nested inside another GlideRecord's while(.next()) loop, with the inner query's filter typically keyed off a value just read from the outer record — the classic shape this pattern always takes.
questions.professionalAnswer: One slow query versus hundreds of fast ones are two completely different diagnoses. A single long line item points to the query itself being expensive. Hundreds of short entries adding up to the real total time points to the same query running over and over, once per row of some outer loop — that's N+1. To confirm it, I'd go straight to the script and look for a GlideRecord query sitting inside another GlideRecord's while(.next()) loop, almost always filtered on something just pulled from the outer record.

Assuming the fix must be indexing rather than eliminating the loop structure itself
Not explaining the specific code shape (nested GlideRecord inside another's loop) to look for
Confusing this signature with a single slow query's signature
keyPoints: One long-duration query entry signals an inherently expensive query
Many short query entries dominating total time signals a repeated query, i.e. N+1
N+1 confirmation means finding a GlideRecord query nested inside another's loop
The fix is restructuring the query, not optimizing the inner query's own speed

Correctly identifies the N+1 pattern from the many-short-queries signature

questions.title: Access That "Used to Work" Breaks After an Unrelated ACL Is Added
questions.prompt: A team reports that a report they've run for months suddenly returns "access denied" after an admin added a new, narrowly-scoped ACL intended only to restrict one unrelated field. Explain precisely why adding that new ACL could break access that had nothing to do with the field it targets, in terms of how multiple applicable ACLs combine.
questions.modelAnswer: Every ACL that's applicable to a given operation on a given table or field must pass, combined with AND — adding a new ACL never weakens what already existed, it only adds one more condition that now has to be satisfied too. If the report reads a field, or the table more broadly, and the new ACL's role, condition, or script doesn't account for the users running that report (even though the new ACL was intended for a completely different, narrower purpose), those users now fail an ACL that didn't exist before, and the report breaks even though nothing about the original, broader ACL changed at all. The fix is to review exactly which operation and which fields the report actually touches, and check the new ACL's role/condition/script against the users who need the report, rather than assuming the new ACL's narrow intent means it couldn't possibly be the cause.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the AND-across-ACLs behavior in action — a brand-new ACL doesn't have to be about the report's field at all to break the report; it just has to apply to something the report touches and fail for the report's users. I'd start by figuring out exactly which table/field/operation the report reads, then check whether the new ACL applies there and whether the report's users actually satisfy its role, condition, or script. Nine times out of ten, the new ACL's scope turns out to be broader than whoever wrote it intended.
commonMistakes: Assuming the new ACL can't be the cause because it was 'narrowly scoped' or 'unrelated'
Not checking which table/field/operation the report actually reads before investigating
Treating this as a bug in the original ACL rather than an expected consequence of adding a new one
Forgetting that ACLs combine with AND, so any one new failure breaks the whole chain
keyPoints: All applicable ACLs combine with AND; a new ACL only ever adds a condition, never removes one
The new ACL doesn't need to target the report's field directly to break it, only to be applicable to what the report touches
The original, broader ACL is unchanged -- the failure is new because the chain of required checks grew
Diagnosis starts with identifying exactly what the report reads, then checking the new ACL against those users

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the AND relationship as the root cause
Correctly explains why the new ACL doesn't need to target the same field to break access
Describes a sound diagnostic approach
Clear, accurate overall reasoning

questions.title: An Approval Step That Never Resolves
questions.prompt: A flow has been "stuck" at an Approval action for two days with no error thrown. Explain the most likely real cause, how the execution log would confirm it, and why this isn't actually a flow bug in the traditional sense even though the business process is clearly broken.
questions.modelAnswer: The most likely cause is that the Approval action's resolved approver or approval group pill is empty or points to someone who was never meant to approve this record — most commonly because an upstream field the routing logic depends on (an assignment group, a manager lookup) resolved to nothing. The execution log would confirm this directly: the run shows the flow genuinely 'waiting' at the Approval step, not errored, and inspecting the resolved value of the approver/group pill at that step reveals it's empty or points to the wrong person. This isn't a flow bug in the traditional sense because the flow is working exactly as designed — it correctly paused and is correctly waiting for a response to an approval request; the real defect is that nobody was actually notified, so the response it's waiting for will never come. The fix is upstream, in whatever logic resolves the approver, not in the Approval action's own configuration.
questions.professionalAnswer: Nine times out of ten this is an approval routed to an empty group or the wrong person — the execution log shows the run sitting at 'waiting' on the Approval step, and checking the resolved approver pill usually shows exactly that: nothing there, or someone who was never supposed to get it. I'd stress that the flow itself isn't broken — it's doing precisely what it's supposed to do, which is wait. The actual bug is upstream, in whatever logic was supposed to resolve a real approver and didn't.
commonMistakes: Assuming a stuck approval must mean the flow itself has an error
Not checking the resolved approver/group pill's actual value at the approval step
Treating the fix as something to apply to the Approval action itself rather than the upstream resolution logic
Missing that the execution log will show 'waiting,' not an error state
keyPoints: The likely cause is an empty or incorrectly resolved approver/group pill
The execution log shows 'waiting' at the approval step, confirming no error occurred
The flow is behaving exactly as designed -- it's waiting for a response that will never come
The real fix is in the upstream logic that resolves the approver, not the Approval action itself

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the likely cause (empty/misrouted approver)
Correctly describes how the execution log confirms it
Correctly explains why this isn't a traditional flow bug
Clear, accurate overall reasoning

questions.title: A Null Data Pill That Isn't a Bug in the Pill Itself
questions.prompt: A flow triggers on record creation and three steps later references a related record that resolves to an empty data pill, with no error. Explain the real, common cause of this specific failure pattern, and the diagnostic step that confirms it rather than assuming the field "should" have had a value.
questions.modelAnswer: The common real cause is a timing or record-lifecycle problem: the flow references a related record in a state that no longer exists by the time that later step actually runs — most often because the related record was deleted, reassigned, or changed between the trigger firing and the referencing step executing, several steps and potentially real elapsed time later. The data pill doesn't error in this situation; it simply resolves to nothing, because ServiceNow dutifully looked for the relationship at the moment the step ran and found nothing there. The diagnostic step is to open the execution log for that specific run, locate the exact step, and look at what the pill actually held at that moment, rather than assuming the field 'should' have had a value based on what was true at trigger time — the whole point is that the state at trigger time and the state several steps later aren't guaranteed to be the same.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is almost always a timing problem, not a pill bug — something about the related record changed or disappeared between the trigger firing and that later step actually running, so the pill correctly resolves to nothing at the moment it's evaluated. I wouldn't trust my assumption about what the field 'should' hold; I'd open the execution log for that run, go to that exact step, and look at what the pill actually held right then. That's the only way to confirm it rather than guess.
commonMistakes: Assuming the data pill itself is broken or misconfigured
Debugging based on what the field 'should' have held rather than what the execution log actually shows
Not considering the time gap between trigger and the failing step as a real-world opportunity for the record to change
Looking at the flow's design instead of a specific run's execution log
keyPoints: A null pill with no error usually means a timing/record-lifecycle problem, not a pill bug
The referenced record changed or was deleted between the trigger and the later step
The execution log shows exactly what the pill held at the moment that step ran
Diagnosis means reading the actual logged value, not assuming what 'should' have been there

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the timing/record-lifecycle cause
Correctly describes the execution-log diagnostic step
Clear, accurate overall reasoning

questions.title: An If/Else Branch That's Silently Wrong
questions.prompt: An If/Else action in a flow is consistently sending records down the wrong branch, with no error thrown anywhere. Explain the most common real cause of this specific symptom, and exactly what you would inspect in the execution log to confirm it.
questions.modelAnswer: The most common real cause is a data type mismatch in the comparison: a number field compared against a string value, or a choice field compared against plain text that doesn't exactly match the underlying choice value stored on the record. Because the comparison itself is syntactically valid, it doesn't throw an error — it just quietly evaluates to the opposite of what the flow builder intended, sending every record down the unexpected branch consistently rather than intermittently. To confirm it, I'd open a specific run's execution log, find the If/Else step, and inspect the actual resolved values on both sides of the comparison exactly as the flow engine saw them at runtime — this almost always reveals one side formatted or typed differently than assumed (for example, the choice field's underlying value versus its display label, or a number resolved as a string).
questions.professionalAnswer: Nine times out of ten this is a type mismatch — comparing a number to a string, or a choice field against text that doesn't match its actual underlying value. It never errors because the comparison is valid, it just evaluates wrong every time, consistently. I'd pull up a specific run, open the If/Else step in the execution log, and look at exactly what both sides of the comparison actually resolved to — that almost always shows one side in a different shape than I assumed.
commonMistakes: Assuming the If/Else logic itself (the condition structure) must be wrong rather than a data type mismatch
Comparing a choice field's display label to its underlying stored value without realizing the distinction
Not inspecting the actual resolved values on both sides of the comparison in the execution log
Treating a consistently-wrong branch the same as an intermittent failure, missing the type-mismatch signature
keyPoints: A data type mismatch is the most common cause of a silently wrong If/Else branch
The comparison never errors, it just evaluates in the opposite of the intended direction
The execution log's resolved values on both sides of the comparison reveal the mismatch
A choice field's display value vs. its underlying value is a common specific culprit

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies data type mismatch as the likely cause
Correctly describes inspecting resolved values in the execution log
Clear, accurate overall reasoning

questions.title: Diagnosing an IntegrationHub REST Step Failure in a Flow
questions.prompt: A flow's IntegrationHub REST step is failing intermittently in production. Name the two realistic failure modes that dominate this kind of failure, how the execution log distinguishes between them, and why you should read that step's actual logged error before re-checking the flow's own logic.
questions.modelAnswer: The two realistic failure modes are an expired or invalidated Connection & Credential Alias (an authentication problem on the ServiceNow side) and the external system itself being unreachable or returning an error response (a problem on the far end, outside ServiceNow's control). The execution log shows the failure directly attached to the REST step, and the distinction is visible in the error itself: an authentication error points specifically to the alias, while a timeout or an HTTP error response coming back from the external system points to that system rather than to anything in the flow's own configuration. Reading that step's actual logged error first matters because the flow's own logic (the steps, the branching, the data pills feeding into the request) is usually not the problem in this kind of failure at all — starting there wastes time re-litigating logic that's already correct, when the real fix is renewing a credential or escalating to the external system's own availability.
questions.professionalAnswer: Two realistic causes dominate: the Connection & Credential Alias has expired or gone bad, or the external system itself is down or erroring. The execution log tells you which one directly — an authentication error points at the alias, a timeout or an HTTP error code from the far end points at the external system. I'd always read that error first before touching the flow's own logic, because in this specific failure mode the flow's logic is almost never actually the problem — it's an external dependency, and re-checking the flow wastes time that should go toward fixing the credential or escalating externally.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to reviewing the flow's own steps and data pills before reading the step's logged error
Not distinguishing an authentication failure (alias) from an external system failure in the log
Assuming an intermittent failure must be a flow design flaw rather than an external dependency issue
Missing that the execution log attaches the error directly to the failing REST step
keyPoints: The two dominant failure modes are an expired/invalid Connection & Credential Alias, or the external system failing
An authentication error in the log points to the alias; a timeout/HTTP error points to the external system
The execution log attaches the error directly to the REST step
The flow's own logic is usually not the problem in this failure category

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly names both realistic failure modes
Correctly explains how the execution log distinguishes between them
Correctly explains why the flow's own logic usually isn't the cause
